title: Chapter 63 — The Crotch
paragraphs: The branches grow out of the trunk, and the twigs out of the branches. In the same way, in productive subjects, the chapters grow.

The crotch mentioned on a previous page deserves a mention of its own. It is a notched stick of a peculiar shape, some two feet long, which is inserted upright into the starboard gunwale near the bow, to provide a rest for the wooden end of the harpoon, whose other, naked, barbed end projects at a slant from the prow. In this way the weapon is instantly at hand for its thrower, who snatches it up from its rest as readily as a backwoodsman swings his rifle down from the wall. It is customary to have two harpoons resting in the crotch, called respectively the first and second irons.

But these two harpoons, each by its own cord, are both connected with the line; the object being this: to dart them both, if possible, one instantly after the other into the same whale, so that if, in the coming drag, one should pull out, the other may still keep its hold. It is a doubling of the chances. But it very often happens that, owing to the instantaneous, violent, convulsive running of the whale on receiving the first iron, it becomes impossible for the harpooner, however lightning-quick his movements, to pitch the second iron into him. Nevertheless, since the second iron is already connected with the line, and the line is running, that weapon must at all events be tossed out of the boat in advance, somehow and somewhere; otherwise all hands would be in the most terrible danger. So in such cases it is tumbled into the water, the spare coils of box line (mentioned in a preceding chapter) making this feat, in most instances, prudently possible. But this critical act is not always free of the saddest and most fatal accidents.

Something else you should know: once the second iron has been thrown overboard, it turns into a dangling, sharp-edged menace, darting skittishly about both boat and whale, fouling the lines or slicing them, and causing a tremendous stir in every direction. And as a rule it cannot be secured again until the whale has been properly caught and is a corpse.

Consider, now, how it must be when four boats are all engaging one unusually strong, active, and knowing whale; when, owing to these qualities in him, as well as to the thousand coinciding accidents of such a daring enterprise, eight or ten loose second irons may be dangling about him at once. For, of course, each boat is supplied with several harpoons to bend on to the line should the first one be darted without effect and not recovered. All these particulars are faithfully set down here, as they will not fail to shed light on several most important, however intricate, passages in scenes to be painted later.
